title: A count of 80 after a short night
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; no antibiotic names, doses or durations are given. Your unit’s peritonitis protocol, the fellow and the attending nephrologist decide every order.
intro:
You are the second-year internal medicine resident in the emergency room (ER) of a tertiary hospital in Iloilo City. At 23:10 you see Mrs. Corazon Dela Peña, 52, who has done peritoneal dialysis (PD) for a year as automated PD (APD), with short night dwells on a cycler. Her abdomen has hurt since the afternoon, and this morning’s drained bag was cloudy. She brought the last bag of last night’s cycle.

She has been constipated for four days, takes a histamine-2 receptor antagonist (H2RA) for heartburn, and her potassium has been low on recent tests. The exit site is clean and the tunnel is not tender. The ER laboratory reports the bag’s count: 80 white cells/µL, 72% neutrophils. The nephrology fellow is on call from home. The International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD) 2022 recommendations guide the unit’s protocol.

n1.prompt: The ER senior says the count is under 100, so this is not peritonitis. What do you decide?

choices.text: Agree. Give pain relief and send her home to see the PD unit in the morning.
choices.feedback: Pain with a cloudy bag already meets one ISPD criterion, and a PD patient with cloudy effluent is presumed to have peritonitis until proven otherwise (1C). Sending her home loses a night of treatment.
choices.then: You call the fellow before she leaves. The fellow asks you to admit her and start the protocol.

choices.text: Treat it as peritonitis: neutrophils above 50% count, even under 100. Culture, then the protocol.
choices.feedback: ISPD 2022 diagnoses peritonitis with two of three: pain or cloudy effluent, a count above 100/µL after a dwell of at least 2 hours with more than 50% neutrophils, or a positive culture (1C). Her dwell was short, so the neutrophil share carries the weight. After short cycler dwells the count runs lower. Send cell count, differential, Gram stain and culture in blood culture bottles before any antibiotic, call the fellow, and start within the hour.

choices.text: Admit her, send cultures, and repeat the count after a proper 2-hour dwell before deciding on antibiotics.
choices.feedback: The cultures are right, but waiting hours to treat is not. Cloudy effluent is treated as peritonitis until the diagnosis is confirmed or excluded (1C).
choices.then: The fellow asks you to start the protocol now, without waiting for the repeat count.

choices.text: Start oral antibiotics now and send the effluent in the morning.
choices.feedback: Antibiotics before sampling make a culture-negative result likely and leave the team treating blind. ISPD sets culture-negative episodes below 15% of a unit’s total (1C), and its preferred route is intraperitoneal (1B).
choices.then: The fellow stops the oral dose. You send the effluent first, then start the unit protocol.

n2.prompt: The fellow asks what the protocol you are starting must cover. What do you say?

choices.text: Gram-positive bacteria only, since most episodes come from touch contamination.
choices.feedback: Most do, but ISPD recommends covering both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria (1C). Her constipation, low potassium and acid-suppressing medicine all raise the chance of a bowel source.
choices.then: The fellow points you to the unit’s full empirical regimen and the antifungal prophylaxis.

vitals.rx: IP gram-positive + gram-negative cover; antifungal prophylaxis

choices.text: An intravenous antibiotic you remember from the ward, at the dose you recall for sepsis.
choices.feedback: ISPD prefers the intraperitoneal (IP) route when compatibility and stability allow (1B). Drugs and doses come from the unit protocol, never from memory.
choices.then: The fellow reads you the unit protocol and you start it as written.

vitals.rx: IP gram-positive + gram-negative cover; antifungal prophylaxis

choices.text: The unit’s empirical protocol, intraperitoneal, both gram types, antifungal prophylaxis.
choices.feedback: ISPD recommends center-specific regimens covering both groups (1C), the intraperitoneal route (1B), and antifungal prophylaxis whenever a PD patient gets antibiotics (1B). The baseline lets you judge the response day by day. Drugs and doses as the protocol writes them; also check for a surgical abdomen and record the baseline count, weight and drain volumes.

vitals.rx: IP gram-positive + gram-negative cover; antifungal prophylaxis

n3.scene: After a proper dwell, the count is 2,400/µL. The culture grows Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and anaerobes. Her pain has settled into the left lower abdomen.
n3.prompt: What does the culture tell you, and what do you do?

choices.text: Mixed enteric bacteria point to the bowel: call now and ask for a surgeon today.
choices.feedback: The route predicts the microbe. Touch contamination brings skin bacteria; several enteric bacteria, especially with anaerobes, suggest a hole in the bowel and need a surgeon. A rigid abdomen or a culture like this is a stop-and-call finding. Not a contaminated exchange. Adjust the antibiotics to the culture with the fellow; correct the low potassium and treat the constipation.

choices.text: Retrain her exchange technique; a contaminated connection is the usual route.
choices.feedback: That route brings skin bacteria, not this mix. Retraining is useful later, but today the bowel needs a surgeon’s look.
choices.then: The fellow reads the culture and calls the surgeon.

choices.text: Narrow the antibiotics to cover E. coli and wait for her response.
choices.feedback: Adjusting to the culture is right, but narrowing to one organism ignores the anaerobes and the possible surgical source.
choices.then: The fellow asks for the surgeon’s opinion and keeps anaerobic cover in the adjusted regimen.

n4.scene: The surgeon found sigmoid diverticular disease without free air and is following her with you. On day 5 the effluent is still slightly hazy, but the count has fallen every day. She is afebrile and her pain is mild. The ward team asks whether the catheter must come out today.

choices.text: Keep going with no set date; she is improving, so the antibiotics are clearly working.
choices.feedback: Improving is good, but without a named decision day a slow infection drags on and injures the membrane. Set the date in advance.
choices.then: The fellow sets the next decision day with the attending and asks you to chart the count daily.

choices.text: Continue: the count is falling. Chart it daily, set a decision day, plan HD access in case.
choices.feedback: ISPD 2022 defines refractory peritonitis as effluent not clear after 5 days of appropriate antibiotics and recommends removal (1D), but suggests observing longer when the count is falling toward normal (2C). Planning access early keeps a removal from becoming a crisis. Name the next decision day with the attending and the surgeon; temporary hemodialysis access in case the catheter has to come out.

choices.text: Remove the catheter today because it is day 5 and the rule says so.
choices.feedback: Day 5 is the refractory threshold (1D), but ISPD now suggests that a falling count justifies longer observation (2C). Removing it now may end PD that could have been saved.
choices.then: The attending reviews the falling counts and chooses to observe, with a named decision day.

choices.text: Stop the antibiotics now that she feels better.
choices.feedback: Feeling better is not cure. The course length is set by the microbes, per the protocol and the attending, and stopping early invites relapse.
choices.then: The fellow continues the course and sets the next decision day with the attending.

n5.scene: The bag is clear, her pain is gone, and she will finish her course at home on APD.
n5.prompt: What goes into her discharge plan?

choices.text: Address the bowel route, finish the course, write a cloudy-bag plan, and count the episode.
choices.feedback: ISPD suggests avoiding or limiting H2RAs (2C) and avoiding and treating low potassium (2C) to prevent enteric peritonitis. Every episode is a question about the route in, and the unit tracks its rate against the target of no more than 0.40 episodes per year at risk. Review the H2RA with the attending, keep her potassium normal, a bowel plan, a PD nurse home visit, and the unit’s infection review.

choices.text: Retrain her exchange technique and send her home with the rest of the antibiotic course.
choices.feedback: Regular retraining is recommended (1C), but her route was the bowel. The acid-suppressing medicine, the potassium and the constipation are what to fix.
choices.then: The fellow adds the H2RA review, potassium checks and a bowel plan.

choices.text: Nothing extra: the infection has cleared, and her technique was checked last month.
choices.feedback: The risks that let bowel bacteria in are all still there. Without a change, the next episode is waiting.
choices.then: The fellow writes the prevention plan and books the infection review.

end.title: Three months later
end.text: Mrs. Dela Peña is still on APD, with no further episodes. Her heartburn medicine was reviewed, her potassium is checked at every clinic visit, and a laminated cloudy-bag plan hangs beside her cycler. The episode was presented at the unit’s infection review as enteric peritonitis linked to diverticular disease.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Cloudy effluent is peritonitis until proven otherwise. After short cycler dwells, more than 50% neutrophils is strong evidence even with a count under 100.
  • Culture in blood culture bottles before the first antibiotic, then start the unit protocol within the hour: gram-positive and gram-negative cover, intraperitoneal, with antifungal prophylaxis.
  • Several enteric bacteria with anaerobes point to the bowel: call the attending and a surgeon.
  • Follow the count daily and name the decision day; a falling count may justify observing beyond day 5 (2C).
  • Fix the route in: H2RA, low potassium and constipation for enteric episodes.

See Diagnosis, Response and removal and Prevention.
